# Why does a market maker earn anything?

*You'll need the book, the spread, taking and making, and fills (chapter 2), and the fair value and the wall mid
(chapter 3). Fill models are chapter 10's; here it is enough that a backtest has to assume which quotes fill.*

## The story

Put our template alone into Prosperity 3's round 1 and it makes 72,674 credits over three days. Put a second copy of
the same bot into the same market, quoting the same prices, and each copy makes about 41 thousand: 41,352 and 41,848.
With two copies beside it, each makes 27 to 30 thousand (@fig-copies). Nothing about the market changed except that
someone else was offering the same thing at the same price
[(`data/copies.csv`; the method in `IDEAS.md`, "The template against copies of itself")]{.src}.

![The same bot alone, against one copy of itself and against two, on Prosperity 3's round 1. Data: `data/copies.csv`,
from `arena.backtest ... --vs python/bots/template.py`.](../figures/f06_copies.png){#fig-copies
fig-alt="Bar chart: alone 73 thousand; with one copy 41 and 42 thousand; with two copies 27, 29 and 30 thousand."}

Other teams' bots do the same. On Prosperity 4's Osmium, alone and with orders that live one tick (the default mode),
the template makes 55,902 credits in round 1. Against
one of three published teams' bots it keeps 27,658 to 32,492, about half; against all three at once, 15,632, under a
third [(`data/osmium_rivals.csv`)]{.src}. Measured on 13 October, the spread on Osmium was a pie of 55 to 62
thousand credits a round, and the bots in the market split it [(`IDEAS.md`, "The template against the teams' P4
traders in one market")]{.src}.

In round 2 of the same competition, the organisers offered "extra market access" to every team whose bid was above
the median bid: about 20% more quotes in their feed, but not 20% more trades. Baguette Fromage, a team whose round 1
income came from market making and from quoting on empty sides of the book, read it as a trap. More market makers'
quotes in the book could only tighten the spread, and fill the empty sides they were earning on. "Why would a rational
team want to PAY for more market maker competition, let alone have more market maker competition at all (even if for
free)?" They bid zero. The median bid, the organisers announced later, was
50, so at least half the field bid 50 or more for the right to face more competition
[(`references/prosperity4-baguette-fromage/README.md:500-519`)]{.src}. We never tested their reasoning; it follows
from this chapter's idea.

A market maker's income is a rent, and rents are shared.

## The idea

### The spread is a fee for immediacy

Someone who wants to trade *now* crosses the book and pays the spread: they buy at the ask, above the mid, or sell at
the bid, below it. Someone willing to wait posts an order and lets the hurried come to them. The market maker is the
one who waits on both sides at once. Each time a taker buys from its ask and another sells to its bid, it has bought
low and sold high by the width of its quotes, without needing any view of where the price is going.

The Varde rehearsal shows this at small scale (@fig-round-trip): the template's first 400 steps on one product of a
mock round we ran with its own exchange, which quotes in cents and scores in euros; the figure shows euros. Most of its fills are passive, sells above the mid and
buys below it, with some takes among them; its position swings between short 9 and long 6 and keeps coming back to
zero; and its profit climbs in small steps, about €4 over 400 steps, while the price itself drifts down.

![A market maker's first 400 steps: LUMEN, the Varde rehearsal's session 1. Top, the mid and our fills; middle, our
position; bottom, PnL valued at the mid. Data: `data/round_trip.csv`, from the rehearsal portal's fills.](../figures/f05_round_trip.png){#fig-round-trip
fig-alt="Three panels over 400 steps: the price drifts down from 101.5 to 101.2 euros with our buys below and sells above it; our position swings between minus 9 and plus 6 lots; our profit rises steadily to about 4 euros."}

The position matters as much as the fills. A market maker that bought and never sold isn't earning a spread; it is
holding a bet on the price. The income exists only because buys and sells alternate closely enough that the position
keeps returning to zero. Chapter 6 is about what happens when it doesn't.

### One tick of the template's quotes

The template does this with three steps each tick, in `trade_product`: *take* any book order priced at least
`take_edge` better than the fair, *clear* some of the position at prices near the fair, then *make*: quote both sides
around the fair. Take the Kelp tick from chapter 2 again, with no position: 2 lots bid at 2,029 and 23 at 2,028, 6
offered at 2,030 and 25 at 2,032. Kelp's settings are `fair: sized_mid` and `make_edge` 0.5, the rest the defaults
(`python/bots/template.py`, `PARAMS["KELP"]`).

The fair is the sized mid, 2,030. Nothing is a take: the best ask, 2,030, is not a credit below the fair, and the
default `take_edge` is 1. Nothing to clear with no position. The make step puts the bid at the fair less half a tick,
rounded down to 2,029, and the ask at the fair plus half a tick, rounded up to 2,031; neither is more than one tick
inside the best quote on its side (`make_inside` 1), so they stay. With `make_size` unset each quote is the full room
under the limit, 50 lots a side. Run through the template's own functions, the plan for that tick is exactly that: a
bid of 50 at 2,029 and an ask of 50 at 2,031, no takes.

So the bot joins the best bid and sits one tick behind the best ask. If a seller hits 2,029, the bot has bought a credit
below its fair; if a buyer lifts 2,031, it has sold a credit above. Either way the fill is worth one credit a unit at
once, against the fair. Whether it is still worth that later is the next question.

### What can go wrong: the price moves after you trade

If that were the whole story, every market maker would be rich. The catch is what happens after a fill. When a taker
buys from you, you are now short. If the taker knew something, the price rises, and the short loses more than the
spread earned. So the question is not "how wide is the spread" but "how wide is the spread compared with how far the
price moves, on average, in the direction of the trades".

*Trades, Quotes and Prices* (eq. 17.13, PDF p. 345) gives the gain of a patient market maker, per unit traded:

::: {.eq speak="a market maker's gain per unit traded is half the average spread, less how far the price eventually moves in the direction of the trades"}
$$\frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{G}]}{\nu_0 T} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[s]}{2} - \mathcal{R}_\infty$$
:::

In it, [$s$]{speak="s"} is the spread and [$\mathcal{R}_\infty$]{speak="R infinity"} is the long-run *impact*: after a
buy, how far the mid ends up above where it was, on average, and the same for sells with the sign flipped (the book's
eq. 1.9, PDF p. 35). Half the spread is what each fill earns at once; the impact is what the market takes back later.
On the large stock markets the book studies, the two nearly cancel, and without the exchange's rebates the plain
strategy loses (§17.2.2): making markets is a competitive business with thin margins.

### Measuring the margin before writing a bot

Both sides of the formula can be measured from the recorded trades alone, with no bot at all. The diagnose tool,
`arena.diagnose`, does it per product. For every market trade it notes the taker's side, +1 for a trade at or above
the best ask and −1 at or below the best bid, then two numbers against the wall mid: what the taker paid, the side
times the price less the wall mid (the tool prints its negative as the taker's `edge`), and how far the wall mid moved their way 50 ticks later, standing in for the long run. The market maker who
took the other side of every trade earns the first and gives back the second
[(`python/arena/diagnose.py`, its docstring's "Market trades")]{.src}.

![The two parts of the margin per unit, for Prosperity 3's round 1 products (credits) and ABIDES's stock (cents),
against the wall mid. Data: `data/margins.csv`, from `arena.diagnose 1 --data p3` and
`--data data/abides`.](../figures/g04_margins.png){#fig-margins
fig-alt="Horizontal bars per product. Kelp: takers pay 0.93 a unit, the price moves 0.01 against them after, margin plus 0.94. Resin: 1.49 paid, 0.07 taken back, margin plus 1.41. Squid Ink: 0.93 paid, margin plus 0.95. ABIDES: 0.99 cents paid, 1.31 taken back, margin minus 0.32."}

The two cases look like this (@fig-margins). On Prosperity 3's Kelp a taker pays 0.93 credits a unit, and 50 ticks later the
price has moved 0.01 *against* them: the market maker keeps 0.94 a unit. Resin keeps 1.41, Squid Ink 0.95. On ABIDES a
taker pays 0.99 cents a unit and the price then moves 1.31 their way: the market maker loses 0.32 a unit
[(`data/margins.csv`)]{.src}. On Prosperity 4's round 1 the margins are larger in credits because the spreads are wider,
7.93 on Osmium and 3.78 on Pepper Root, but as a share of the spread they are the same kind of number: 0.49 and 0.37,
against Kelp's 0.41 and ABIDES's −0.21 [(`data/margins.csv`)]{.src}.

That one measurement says whether plain market making can work on a market at all. Prosperity is the easy case, the
textbook's "zero-intelligence" market where takers know nothing: trades barely move the price. A second sign agrees.
On Prosperity a trade's side says almost nothing about the next trade's: the correlation of consecutive signs is 0.09
to 0.13, against 0.37 to 0.93 on NASDAQ stocks [(`IDEAS.md`, "Does market making pay here, by the textbook's
test?")]{.src}. On ABIDES it is 0.36: trades come in runs, as they do when someone large is working an order
[(`data/margins.csv`)]{.src}. Chapter 5 is about the market on the other side of that number.

The margin is an upper bound for one bot, not a forecast. It is what the *average* taker leaves on the table against
the wall mid, before anyone competes for it and before any fill rule. The template's own passive fills on Kelp earn
0.69 credits a unit and keep it for 500 ticks (chapter 5's markout figure), less than 0.94; we haven't measured why.

### So where does the income come from?

Three things decide it, and you control only some of them:

- **How much uninformed flow there is,** traders who cross the spread for reasons that don't predict the price. They
  are the market maker's customers. You can't create them.
- **How many others compete for them.** The story: a second bot at your price takes a little under half. Quoting a
  little better than the others wins the trades, but each step inside the spread gives away margin.
- **How well you avoid the informed.** Quoting further from the fair, pulling quotes when the book looks dangerous,
  or skewing them against your position (moving both quotes so the side that adds to it is the less attractive)
  all trade a little income for safety. Chapter 5 is about the informed, chapter 6 about the position.

### Competition is the spread's other side

Baguette Fromage's reasoning is the textbook's, in reverse. If market makers earn more than their risk, others join,
undercut each other's quotes and narrow the spread until the margin is thin. The large stock markets are at the end
of that process; Prosperity's bots aren't, which is why its margins are a third or more of the spread. In a contest
every team is a potential market maker in the same book, if the book is shared. Each one that quotes at your price
splits the flow, and each one that quotes inside you takes it.

The mechanism is the matching rule of chapter 2. An incoming order trades with the best price first, so a bid one
credit higher than yours is hit before yours is. Quoting a tick inside the others, *pennying*, wins the next trades and
gives up a tick of margin on each; the others can do the same, and the margin goes down a tick at a time until one of
them would rather wait. That is why the template's make step has two limits, a distance from the fair it won't come
inside (`make_edge`) and a number of ticks inside the best quote it won't go beyond (`make_inside`): it competes for
the trades, but not past the point where they stop paying. On the Kelp tick above, the bot joined the best bid rather
than bidding 2,030, which would have bought from the 2,030 ask at its own fair and earned nothing.

Osmium shows the rest of the arithmetic. Against one team's bot the template kept 49 to 58% of what it made alone, and
against three, 28% [(`data/osmium_rivals.csv`)]{.src}. Three rivals didn't leave it a quarter each: they quote at
different distances, take differently and hold different positions, so the pie isn't cut evenly, and a replay can't
say how the takers themselves would have reacted to four market makers instead of one.

One caution about @fig-copies: between them the copies make a little more than one bot alone (83 and 86 thousand
against 73). Don't read anything into that: a replay can't let the market react to two bots instead of one, so the
total isn't something a real market would pay. Read each copy's share, which is what would be scored. And a share
depends on how the exchange breaks ties between two orders at the same price, which a replay also has to assume.

::: {.callout-note title="What would differ on another market"}
On ABIDES the margin is negative, −0.32 cents a unit, because value and momentum agents move the price after their
trades; the template as committed loses there under every fill model (chapter 5). On the Varde rehearsal's exchange a fee on
every order placed, not just every lot traded, took 28% of the gross: a cost the margin in this chapter doesn't see
(chapter 12). Prosperity 4's Osmium has a margin eight times Kelp's in credits and a
similar share of its spread. The formula is the same everywhere; the measurement is per market and per product.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
Measuring [$\mathbb{E}[s]/2 - \mathcal{R}_\infty$]{speak="half the spread less the impact"} from the data is
estimating a baseline's expected reward before you train anything: if it is negative, no amount of tuning a plain
market maker will fix it. The copies are a multi-agent effect: the reward is shared, so a policy that looks good alone
is worth less in a population of similar policies. Where it breaks: the margin is measured on other traders' trades,
and your quotes change who trades with you. A bot that quotes tighter than everyone gets more of the informed flow too.
:::
